ca_eagles_peak_area.blurb: Eagles Peak Area is the westernmost cluster of rock at Dixon Lake, a city park in north Escondido, where the main trail ends on top of formations looking down over town. Fourteen short trad and top-rope lines work cracks, overhanging faces and small boulders. Grades start around 5.7 and reach 5.12, with the bulk in the 5.10 to 5.11 range, so it suits climbers stepping up from moderates more than complete beginners. The headline route here carries a runout rating, and the harder lines are steep and physical for their height. Expect quick sessions on compact stone rather than a long day of cragging.

ca_lone_pine_peak.blurb: Lone Pine Peak is a big white-granite mountain rising above the town of Lone Pine in the Eastern Sierra, often mistaken for Mount Whitney from the valley. The fourteen routes here are mostly long alpine lines, with some trad, a winter ice and mixed pair, an aid route and one scramble. Technical grades run from about 5.6 to 5.11, and several climbs are many pitches long, so expect a full mountain day with a committing descent. The north side is reached from the Whitney Portal road, while the longer south-face routes use dirt roads and the Stone House area. This is a destination for experienced alpine parties.

ca_sector_b.blurb: Sector B is the tallest wall in The Ravine, a small bouldering venue near Mammoth Lakes at about 7,500 feet. Fourteen problems fill it, nearly all easy: most sit around V0 with a couple of V1 to V3 lines, plus one standout hard problem near V8. The wall faces southwest and takes sun for most of the day, so it can be hot in any season, and snow keeps the Ravine mostly a warm-weather stop. Several landings are rocky and uneven, so bring pads and spot carefully. The walk from the road is short, heading north up the ravine with the wall on your right.

ca_sanctuary_the.blurb: The Sanctuary is a hidden sport crag on a ridgeline above Coon Creek and the South Fork Trinity drainage in Northwest California, tucked away from roads and trails. Fourteen bolted routes run from about 5.10 into the low 5.13 range, with a spread of 5.10s through 5.12s. The wall faces south and west and dries quickly. It sits only minutes from Trinity Aretes, which makes it a handy backup when that crag is crowded or cold. The setting is quiet and wooded, with plenty of wildlife around.

ca_thunderbird_wall.blurb: Thunderbird Wall is a popular east-facing wall in the Central Pinnacles of Holcomb Valley, just north of Big Bear Lake in the San Bernardino Mountains at roughly 7,500 feet. Fourteen routes mix sport, trad and top-rope, with grades from about 5.7 to 5.10, most of them in the 5.8 to 5.10 band. It is known for a good variety of well-protected moderates, including short bolted lines and a few crack climbs. The back side of the formation is a separate wall. Reach it from the base of neighbouring Claim Jumper Wall or Gunsmoke Wall by a short trail and a little scrambling.

ca_west_wall_inner_jane_s_addiction_area.blurb: This is the inner east-facing side of the West Wall in the Hall of Horrors, in the Sheep Pass part of Joshua Tree National Park at about 4,300 feet. Fourteen routes cover trad, sport and a couple of top-ropes, mostly crack and face lines. Two easy cracks start things off, but the real draw is steeper climbing: most routes fall in the 5.11 range, with a few 5.10s and some 5.12s. Most of the routes sit right of centre in the valley between the two main formations, across from a well-known crack. The Hall of Horrors handles crowds well because its separate faces spread climbers out.
ca_west_wall_inner_jane_s_addiction_area.approach: From the parking area, go right past the end of the East Wall, then cut left into the broad valley between the two main formations. The wall is on your right. Approaches in the Hall of Horrors are typically 20 minutes or less.

ca_south_flank.blurb: South Flank is a small, busy cliff on the south side of Daff Dome in Tuolumne Meadows, Yosemite, at about 8,500 feet. Fourteen routes of polished golden granite are mostly trad, with a handful of sport lines and top-ropes. Most are short, easy-to-moderate cracks from about 5.5 to 5.8, and the little crack lines draw crowds on weekends. Beyond those sit runout face climbing near 5.10 and bolted routes in the 5.10 to 5.11 range. Most of the face looks southeast and catches sun from mid-morning to early afternoon in summer. A treed gully trail climbs to the base in about ten minutes.
ca_south_flank.approach: A trail climbs a low-angle treed gully to the base; allow about 10 minutes.

ca_staying_power_towers.blurb: Staying Power Towers is a sector of the Inner Gorge in Owens River Gorge near Bishop, around 5,450 feet in dry Eastern Sierra desert. Thirteen of its fourteen routes are bolted, with one trad line, and the face and crack climbing is clean, delicate and fingery. Grades start near 5.9 and centre on the 5.11 range, with a few 5.10s and a pair of 5.12s, so it rewards climbers who are comfortable on technical terrain. Shade is scarce, which makes early starts and plenty of water worthwhile in warm weather.
